description_full: VTEX, together with its subsidiaries, provides software-as-a-service digital commerce platform for enterprise brands and retailers. It provides VTEX platform that enables customers to execute commerce strategy, including building online stores, and integrating and managing orders across channels, as well as creating marketplaces to sell products from third-party vendors. The company also offers customer support services; and optional services, such as project management, solutions architecting, and implementation consulting services. It serves its products to home appliances, apparel and accessories, beauty and health, electronics, grocery, department stores, and toys and hobbies, as well as home, furniture, and decoration markets. The company has operations in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, France, Italy, Mexico, Peru, Portugal, Romania, Spain, the United Kingdom, the United States, and internationally. VTEX was founded in 2000 and is headquartered in Grand Cayman, Cayman Islands.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $211K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers. Each employee generates $28K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $15K per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: VTEX is a small-cap technology business with a $643M market cap on $241M of annual revenue.
Returns on capital run at 39% against a 10% cost of capital — a 29-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 77% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $32M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.67× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 9.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 48% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
